food.text: Spanish and Portuguese explorers of the 16th and 17th centuries noted flourishing communities along the Amazon and its tributaries. Their reports described large, well-fed populations along the bluffs, surrounded by orchards on the uplands and seasonal fields in the floodplains.
food.source_title: Pre-Columbian agriculture in the Amazon Basin

food.text: In the first decades of the 17th century, Jesuits in what is now southern Brazil, Paraguay, and the Argentine provinces of Misiones and Corrientes improved the cultivation technique of yerba mate. They also exported it.

Brazilian cooking speaks of culinária crioula for the notable influence African cuisine had on colonial Brazilian society. Enslaved Africans adapted their cooking to local ingredients such as mandioca and milho. They also brought across the Atlantic azeite de dendê, cuscuz, the coconut, and coffee.

In 1542 Francisco de Orellana became the first European to travel the length of the Amazon River. The BBC's Unnatural Histories presents evidence that he was correct, rather than exaggerating, that a complex civilization was flourishing along the river in the 1540s, with agriculture advanced enough to support prosperous and populous societies. It is believed that this civilization was later devastated by diseases spread from Europe, such as smallpox.

Some 5 million people may have lived in the Amazon region in AD 1500, divided between dense coastal settlements such as Marajó and inland dwellers. One estimate, based on projections of food production, suggests over 8 million people lived there in 1492. By 1900 the native indigenous population had fallen to 1 million, and by the early 1980s it was less than 200,000.
To compete with the tea that England sold, Spain put chopped yerba mate on sale to make a tea. It became popular in Europe and was known as the "Tea of the Jesuits".
Feijoada is considered today to be the national dish of Brazil. Yet it has its origins in the cuisine of African slaves in colonial Brazil.

The arrival of European settlers brought about the collapse of the Amazon's agricultural systems and the populations they supported. The people did not survive the introduction of European diseases and forced labor: they died of them, and with them died the farming knowledge they carried. Pre-Columbian farming practices were largely forgotten.
food.source_title: Pre-Columbian agriculture in the Amazon Basin

food.text: Casabe is a flatbread eaten across the Caribbean Basin and the Amazon, usually made of bitter cassava, which is toxic before processing: both kinds of cassava contain linamarin, which produces cyanide, and the bitter kind contains much more. The poison has to be removed by extracting the water, since cyanide dissolves in it. European explorers, soldiers, and buccaneers adopted casabe in the sixteenth century, and it was produced and traded at large scales, including on Mona Island, which exported over 75 tons a year on slave ships in the 1510s and 1520s. Spanish colonists also planted cassava so they could feed casabe to their indigenous laborers under the encomienda system of forced labor.

Explorers of the 16th and 17th centuries noted the Amazon's flourishing communities, but little historical documentation exists on the population. Conservative estimates place it at 1 or 2 million people, while the highest estimates fix it at between 8 and 10 million.
food.source_title: Pre-Columbian agriculture in the Amazon Basin

art.text: Baroque became the dominant artistic style of colonial Brazil, appearing at the beginning of the 17th century. It was brought by Catholic missionaries, especially Jesuits, who came to catechize and acculturate the native indigenous peoples and to assist the Portuguese in colonizing. Slavery was a fundamental aspect of colonial Brazilian society and the basis of its workforce, and the Portuguese heavily exploited the colony for crops and minerals.

Brazilian Baroque reached its highest originality in Minas Gerais, where a gold rush nurtured a rich and cultured local society. There lived its greatest artists: the painter Manuel da Costa Ataíde and the sculptor-architect Aleijadinho.

Colonial Brazil's architecture ran from 1500, the year of the Portuguese arrival, until Independence in 1822. Colonizers imported European currents, including Renaissance, Mannerism, Baroque, Rococo and Neoclassical, and adapted them to local materials and socioeconomic conditions.

The colony had no court to act as a patron of the arts, and the elites did not bother to build palaces. Because religion strongly influenced daily life, most of the Baroque legacy is sacred art: statuary, painting and carving for churches and convents. The Church used it to impose beliefs and models of conduct on a population made up mostly of non-Christians, indigenous Brazilians and enslaved Africans, who in practice were rarely even considered human beings and were treated as private property, an instrument of exploitation and a source of profit. Its art helped justify slavery and keep the social and political status quo.

Jesuit missionary establishments called Reductions taught religion through art, including sacred plays, music, statuary and painting. José de Anchieta was the first important playwright to emerge from this effort.

Ouro Preto holds the best examples of Baroque architecture in Brazil, with ornate forms, rounded corners and paintings incorporated into the walls. It has 13 churches, 11 chapels, major museums, ancient bridges and well-preserved houses.

Minas Gerais was also the birthplace of a proto-Neoclassical school of music and literature. Its composers included Lobo de Mesquita and Francisco Gomes da Rocha, alongside the poets Tomás Antônio Gonzaga and Cláudio Manuel da Costa.

Agostinho de Jesus and Agostinho da Piedade produced the first known sculptures in Brazil. The first paintings came from Belchior Paulo, João Filipe Bettendorff, Ricardo do Pilar and a few others, all working under Baroque influence.

Many Catholic church buildings were destroyed during the Dutch occupation of northeast Brazil from 1630 to 1654, and the colonial administrative center of Salvador was largely ruined. After the Dutch were expelled in the mid-17th century, a large-scale effort followed to restore the old structures and build new ones, with Borromini's influence adding movement to façades through arched openings, railings, reliefs and oculi.

Recife was transformed under Count John Maurice of Nassau, who governed from 1637 to 1643. Through embankments and the construction of bridges, canals and forts, he turned the old port of Olinda into a city.

In Belém do Pará, Antônio José Landi designed the Santana Church (1760–1782), a rare centralized building in colonial Brazil. It has a Greek cross plan with a dome, and he also designed the Grão-Pará General Governors' Palace.
The Dutch governor John Maurice of Nassau invited artists and scientists to the colony of Dutch Brazil. His aim was to help promote Brazil and increase immigration.

Ouro Preto's best-preserved residence is the Casa dos Contos, built in 1780. This beige and white three-story building has a stone watering trough for horses in the back yard, and dark flagstone cubicles where slaves lived.

war.text: From 1630 the Dutch Republic conquered almost half of Brazil's settled European area at the time. The Dutch West India Company had its headquarters in Recife, which was also the capital of the colony. The colony was known as New Holland.

Portugal repelled Dutch attempts to secure Brazil, Angola and Mozambique during the Dutch–Portuguese War. Because of the commodity at the center of the conflict, the war was nicknamed the Spice War. It was a global struggle in which the Dutch companies invaded Portuguese colonies in the Americas, Africa and the East Indies.
Through wars against the French, the Portuguese slowly expanded their territory in Brazil. They took Rio de Janeiro in 1567 and, to the northwest, São Luís in 1615.

In 1621 the twelve-year peace treaty between the Dutch and the Habsburgs expired. The United Netherlands immediately chartered a Dutch West India Company, and the Dutch–Portuguese War resumed. Through the new company the Dutch began interfering with Spanish and Portuguese colonies in the Americas.

Dutch privateers plundered the Brazilian coast after Philip II prohibited commerce with Dutch ships. They sacked Salvador in 1604 and removed large amounts of gold and silver before a joint Spanish-Portuguese fleet recaptured the town.

The tide turned against the Dutch in Brazil when the Portuguese won a significant victory at the Second Battle of Guararapes in 1649. The Dutch surrendered on 26 January 1654 and signed a capitulation, but only as a provisional pact.
Portuguese military expeditions were sent to the Amazon River basin rainforest. There they conquered competing English and Dutch strongholds, and founded villages and forts from 1669.
In 1680 the Portuguese reached the far southeast and founded Colônia do Sacramento on the bank of the Río de la Plata. It lay in the Banda Oriental region, in present-day Uruguay.

After the Battle of Mbwila, many people, including nobles and members of the royal family, were captured, and some were enslaved and shipped across the sea to Brazil. The sons of Princess Aqualtune, who had led a battalion in the battle, Ganga Zumba and Ganga Zona, and their sister Sabina, turned up enslaved on an engenho, a sugar cane plantation, in Pernambuco before 1670. They led a rebellion there, escaped, and founded Quilombo dos Palmares, a Maroon nation that controlled large areas of northeast Brazil. What happened to most of the other captives is unknown.
The Dutch attacked Bahia twice in 1638, but the Portuguese fought both attacks back. By 1641, however, the Dutch had captured São Luís, giving them control of northwestern Brazil.
The Dutch captured Salvador again in May 1624. Eleven months later they surrendered the city to a Luso-Spanish armada.

The Spanish conquered the Banda Oriental region in 1777. Yet this was in vain, because the Treaty of San Ildefonso, signed in the same year, confirmed Portuguese sovereignty over all lands gained through its expansion. It thus created most of the current Brazilian southeastern border.
The Spanish tried to stop Portuguese expansion into territory they said belonged to them under the 1494 Treaty of Tordesillas. That division of the New World was made by Pope Alexander VI.

literature.text: One of the first extant documents that might be considered Brazilian literature is the letter Pero Vaz de Caminha wrote to Manuel I of Portugal. It describes what Brazil looked like in 1500. Journals of voyagers and descriptive treatises on Portuguese America then dominated literary production for the next two centuries.

One of the first surviving documents that might count as Brazilian literature is the letter of Pero Vaz de Caminha to Manuel I of Portugal. It describes what Brazil looked like in 1500. Some treat it as the birth of Brazilian literature.
tags: Carta de Pero Vaz de Caminha

literature.text: For two centuries after Caminha's letter, voyagers' journals and descriptive treatises on Portuguese America dominated what was written. Early Brazilian literature largely followed the literary trends of Portugal.

Gregório de Matos was a 17th-century lawyer from Salvador who produced a large body of satirical, religious and secular poetry. He drew heavily on Baroque influences, including the Spanish poets Luis de Góngora and Francisco de Quevedo.

Travel accounts dominated early writing about Portuguese America, including well-known works by Jean de Léry and Hans Staden. Staden's story of his encounter with the Tupi Indians on the coast of São Paulo was extraordinarily influential for European conceptions of the New World.

Gregório de Matos, a 17th-century lawyer from Salvador, produced a sizable amount of satirical, religious, and secular poetry. He drew heavily from Baroque influences such as the Spanish poets Luis de Góngora and Francisco de Quevedo.

When Brazil became a Portuguese colony, a "Jesuit Literature" arose, whose main name was Father António Vieira. A Portuguese Jesuit, he became one of the most celebrated Baroque writers of the Portuguese language.

Hans Staden told the story of his encounter with the Tupi Indians on the coast of São Paulo. His account was extraordinarily influential in shaping European ideas of the New World. It sits among the well-known travel accounts that dominated early writing about Brazil.
Basílio da Gama wrote an epic poem celebrating the conquest of the Guarany Missions by the Portuguese. It is one of the few explicitly literary works surviving from colonial Brazil.

In the mid-18th century, Neoclassicism following the Italian style was widespread in Brazil. Literature was often produced by members of temporary or semi-permanent academies, and most of it was in the pastoral genre.

The most important literary centre in colonial Brazil was the prosperous, gold-mining region of Minas Gerais, where a proto-nationalist movement had begun to thrive. Its most important poets were Cláudio Manuel da Costa, Tomás António Gonzaga, Alvarenga Peixoto and Manuel Inácio da Silva Alvarenga, all of them involved in an uprising against the colonial power. As a consequence, Gonzaga and Costa were exiled to Africa.

In the mid-18th century, neoclassicism spread through Brazil, and literature was often produced by members of temporary or semi-permanent academies. The most important literary centre was the gold-mining region of Minas Gerais. Poets such as Cláudio Manuel da Costa, Tomás António Gonzaga, Alvarenga Peixoto and Manuel Inácio da Silva Alvarenga were all involved in an uprising against the colonial power. As a consequence, Gonzaga and Costa were exiled to Africa.

Gregório de Matos wrote a series of satirical poems of a homosexual nature about his political adversaries. This is why he is seen as the starting point of a tradition of LGBTQ literature in Brazil, dating back to the seventeenth century.

Afro-Brazilian oral traditions of histories and narratives can be traced back to the 16th century, when African slaves were brought across the Atlantic to work in the Portuguese colonies. Written forms did not appear until the 19th century.
Brazil's tradition of LGBTQ literature dates back to the 17th century. The poet Gregório de Matos wrote satirical poems with homosexual references, which are the earliest roots of that tradition.

science.text: Around 1783, the Portuguese naturalist Alexandre Rodrigues Ferreira led an expedition sent by Portugal's prime minister, the Marquis of Pombal. His task was to explore and identify Brazilian fauna, flora and geology. It is described as the first firm attempt at creating a Brazilian science establishment.

In 1772, the Sociedade Scientifica was founded in Rio de Janeiro. It was one of the first learned societies of both Brazil and the Portuguese Empire, and it appeared even before the Science Academy of Lisbon was established in 1779. It lasted only until 1794.
In 1797, the first botanic institute in Brazil was founded in Salvador, Bahia. It belonged to the late 18th-century wave of first attempts to build a scientific establishment in the colony.

In 1792, Portuguese authorities issued a decree creating the Real Academia de Artilharia, Fortificação e Desenho in Rio de Janeiro. It was a higher education school for teaching the sciences and engineering, and it is the oldest engineering school in Brazil and one of the oldest in Latin America. Today's engineering schools of the Rio de Janeiro Federal University and the Military Institute of Engineering grew from it.
tags: Real Academia de Artilharia, Fortificação e Desenho

science.text: During the government of Count John Maurice of Nassau (1637-1643), Recife saw great urban works: embankments, bridges, canals and forts. These works transformed the old port of Olinda into a city.

The natural history collections gathered by Alexandre Rodrigues Ferreira's expedition were lost to the French when Napoleon invaded Portugal. They were transported to Paris by Étienne Geoffroy Saint-Hilaire.

politics.text: The Inconfidência Mineira of 1789 was an unsuccessful separatist movement in colonial Brazil. Its external inspiration was the independence of the thirteen British colonies in North America, which impressed the intellectual elite of Minas Gerais. Its internal cause was the decline of gold mining and the burden of the derrama tax.

On 23 April 1500, the navigator Pedro Álvares Cabral landed on the coast of the land now known as Brazil, and the Portuguese claimed it for the first time. Permanent Portuguese settlement followed in 1534. Over the next 300 years they slowly expanded west until they had established nearly all of modern Brazil's borders.
politics.source_title: History of the Empire of Brazil

politics.text: In 1580, King Philip II of Spain invaded Portugal after a succession crisis, brought on by King Sebastião's death in a disastrous Portuguese attack on Alcácer Quibir in Morocco in 1578. Philip seized the Portuguese crown and Portuguese territories such as Brazil. The union ended in 1640, when João IV was proclaimed king of Portugal and the Portuguese Restoration War began. Spain recognised the end of the Iberian Union in 1668.

From 1630 to 1654, the Dutch Republic controlled a colony in the northeast of modern Brazil, called Dutch Brazil or New Holland. The Dutch conquered almost half of Brazil's settled European area at the time. The capital and the headquarters of the Dutch West India Company were in Recife.

The Tamoio had been allied with the French since the settlement of France Antarctique. Mem de Sá's forces had expelled the French, Huguenot, Scottish Calvinist and slave forces by 1560, burning their fortifications and villages. Jesuits Manuel de Nóbrega and José de Anchieta took part in attacks on the Tamoios and spied on their resources. From 1565 through 1567 Mem de Sá destroyed France Antarctique at Guanabara Bay, and he and his nephew Estácio de Sá established the city of Rio de Janeiro in 1567. By 1575 the Tamoios had been subdued and essentially were extinct.

Even before the Restoration War ended, the Portuguese crown established the Overseas Council in 1643. It had been conceived in 1642 on the short-lived model of the Council of India (1604–1614). It became the governing body for most of the Portuguese overseas empire, with exceptions including North Africa, Madeira and the Azores.

After the restructuring of the Governorate General of Brazil in 1621, Portuguese America was divided into the State of Brazil and the State of Maranhão. In 1751, Maranhão became the mega-colony State of Grão-Pará and Maranhão. In 1772, it was split into Grão-Pará and Rio Negro, and Maranhão and Piauí.

The Inconfidência Mineira conspirators shared a goal of independence but not a program. Some were republicans and others monarchists, and some favored abolishing slavery while others thought it impractical. Many wanted a republic that would keep the ownership of slaves intact. The plotters included poets Cláudio Manuel da Costa and Tomás Antônio Gonzaga, and José Álvares Maciel, a philosopher and chemistry student.

The governor of Dutch Brazil, John Maurice of Nassau, invited artists and scientists to the colony to help promote Brazil and increase immigration. The colony's capital was Mauritsstad, which is today part of Recife.

In 1594, Philip II, who was king of Spain and, from 1580, of Portugal, allowed Dutch ships bound for Brazil to sail together once a year in a fleet of twenty ships. This came during the Eighty Years' War, when Dutch raiders were attacking Spanish lands, colonies and ships.

Under the Twelve Years' Truce signed in 1609, the Dutch Republic was allowed to trade with Portuguese settlements in Brazil. Portugal's small size and population meant it needed foreign participation in its empire's colonization and commerce. As part of the truce, the Dutch also agreed to delay founding a West India Company.

The Portuguese founded the Colony of Santíssimo Sacramento in 1680, gaining substantial territory in South America. During the 18th century, the Portuguese and the Spanish disputed the colony for the major part of the century, creating uneasy conditions there.

Tiradentes was the most enthusiastic propagandist of the Inconfidência Mineira. He took full responsibility for the conspiracy, and for that reason, when Queen Maria I commuted the death sentences of the other condemned conspirators to perpetual banishment, his was not commuted because his activities involved aggravated circumstances. He was imprisoned in Rio de Janeiro and hanged there on 21 April 1792. Afterwards his body was torn into pieces, which were sent to Vila Rica to be displayed in the places where he had propagated his revolutionary ideas. The anniversary of his death is a national holiday in Brazil.

By the end of the truce, the Dutch had gained over half of the carrying trade between Brazil and Europe. The northern Netherlands operated 29 sugar refineries by 1622, versus 3 in 1595. In 1621, the United Netherlands immediately chartered a Dutch West India Company.

philosophy.text: The Spanish and Portuguese empires in South America gathered native populations into communities called "Indian reductions" (reducciones in Spanish, reduções in Portuguese). Their objectives were to impart Christianity and European culture. The Jesuit missions among the Guaraní were one such type of settlement, in the area where Argentina, Brazil and Paraguay now meet.

Later observers have judged the Jesuit missions among the Guaraní very differently. Some called them an experiment in "socialist theocracy" or a rare example of "benign colonialism". Others said that "the Jesuits took away the Indians' freedom, forced them to radically change their lifestyle, physically abused them, and subjected them to disease".

António Vieira was a Portuguese Jesuit priest, preacher, diplomat and philosopher who grew up in colonial Brazil. He came to the colony in 1614 with his parents and was educated at the Jesuit college at Bahia. He entered the Jesuit novitiate in 1625 and was teaching rhetoric at eighteen.

The Jesuits attempted to create a "state within a state" in the Río de la Plata missions. The native peoples, guided by the Jesuits, would remain autonomous and isolated from Spanish colonists and Spanish rule. The reductions reached a maximum population of 141,182 in 1732, spread over 30 missions in Brazil, Paraguay and Argentina.

In 1654 António Vieira sailed to Lisbon to plead the cause of the Indians. In April 1655 he obtained royal decrees that placed the missions under the Society of Jesus, with himself as superior. The decrees also prohibited the enslavement of the natives except in certain specified cases.

Brazil did not establish universities until 1920, so colonial higher education was limited to a few clerical institutions, typically founded and directed by the Society of Jesus. As a result, Brazilian Scholasticism never asserted a notable influence. It had almost disappeared by the end of the 18th century.

In 1609, acting under instructions from Philip III, the Spanish governor of Asunción made a deal with the Jesuit Provincial of Paraguay. The Jesuits agreed to set up hamlets along the Paraná river, populated with Indians and kept separate from Spanish towns. In return they were to enjoy a tax holiday for ten years.

At the pope's request, António Vieira drew up a two-hundred-page report on the Inquisition in Portugal. After a judicial inquiry, Pope Innocent XI suspended the Inquisition there for seven years (1674 to 1681). Vieira returned to Brazil in January 1681 and died in Salvador, Bahia, in 1697.

In August 1659, António Vieira signed the Treaty of the Mapuá with various indigenous groups on the Marajó Archipelago. It came during the six years (1655 to 1661) in which he organized the missions over a territory with a coast-line of 400 leagues. Colonists who blamed the Jesuits for the shortage of slaves began to oppose him.

culture.text: In colonial Brazil, blacks and mulattos, whether slaves or freedmen, often joined Catholic religious brotherhoods. Among the most important were the Sisterhood of Our Lady of the Good Death and the Sisterhood of Our Lady of the Rosary of the Black Men. They also served as a link between Catholicism and Afro-Brazilian religions.
tags: Sisterhood of Our Lady of the Good Death
Sisterhood of Our Lady of the Rosary of the Black Men

culture.text: In 1542, Francisco de Orellana reached the Amazon River and named it after the Icamiabas, a tribe of warlike women he claimed to have encountered and fought on the Nhamundá River. The whole basin and region of the Amazon were afterwards named after the river.

Catholicism in colonial Brazil absorbed African influence in its cult of saints. Saints Cosmas and Damian were associated with the ibeji, Saint George with Ogun in Rio de Janeiro, and Saint Barbara with Yansã. These pairings tied Catholic devotion to African orishas.

Governor John Maurice of Nassau invited artists and scientists to Dutch Brazil to help promote the colony and increase immigration. The Dutch controlled part of northeastern Brazil from 1630 to 1654, with their capital and West India Company headquarters in Recife.

The cult of saints of African origin entered Brazilian Catholicism, including Saint Benedict, Saint Elesbaan, Saint Ephigenia and Saint Anthony of Noto. Popular devotion also created new saints, such as the Escrava Anastacia.

In 1619, about 300 couples arrived in Maranhão, around 1000 people in total, led by Estácio da Silveira. It was the first region to receive Azorean settlers in an organised way, and successive waves of Azorean couples followed throughout the 17th century.
